title: Threads & Multithreading
summary: A thread is a path of execution within a process. What threads share, what stays private, and why the process-vs-thread trade-off is one of the most-asked framing questions in OS interviews.

slides.markdown:
A **thread** is a single sequential path of execution — its own program counter, its own stack, its own registers. A process has at least one thread; it can have many, all running within that one process's shared address space.

Why bother with multiple threads instead of multiple processes? Because sharing memory is exactly what a web server handling thousands of simultaneous connections, or a UI keeping the interface responsive while doing background work, actually needs — and threads give you that sharing almost for free, at the cost of needing to coordinate carefully.

slides.sectionTitle: What is a thread? Execution within a process
slides.markdown:
Think of a process as a container — its address space, open files, and other resources — and a thread as one runner moving through that container, executing instructions one at a time. A **single-threaded** process has exactly one runner; a **multi-threaded** process has several runners moving through the same container simultaneously (or concurrently, on a single core).

Each thread needs, at minimum, its own program counter (where it currently is in the code), its own stack (its own call history and local variables), and its own set of CPU register values — because each thread is independently making function calls and doing computation, even though they're all executing the same program's code.

The OS schedules **threads**, not processes, onto CPU cores — a process with three ready threads and one CPU-bound single-threaded process compete for CPU time as four independent schedulable entities, not effectively-one-vs-one.

slides.sectionTitle: What threads share vs what's private to each thread
slides.markdown:
**Shared** across all threads in a process: the code (text segment), global and static variables, the heap, open file descriptors, and the process's PID and other process-level state.

**Private** to each thread: its own stack (local variables, call frames, return addresses), its own program counter, its own CPU register values, and typically its own thread ID and thread-local storage (a small amount of memory explicitly marked as per-thread, even though it lives in the shared address space).

The consequence that drives almost every threading bug: because the heap and globals are shared, one thread writing to a shared variable is immediately visible to every other thread — with no isolation to catch a mistake. That's the entire reason synchronization (locks, atomics) exists as its own topic.

slides.markdown:
![Single-threaded vs multi-threaded address space](assets/single-vs-multithreaded.svg)

The visual point is that adding threads doesn't create new address spaces — the code and heap boxes stay exactly the same size and location, and only the number of stacks grows, one per thread, all carved out of the same overall address space the single-threaded version already had.

slides.sectionTitle: Why use threads: concurrency, responsiveness, cheaper than processes
slides.markdown:
Three concrete reasons threads exist as a tool, not just a concept:

- **Responsiveness**: a GUI app can run its UI-drawing loop on one thread while a slow file download runs on another, so the interface never freezes while waiting on I/O.
- **Parallelism**: on a multi-core machine, genuinely independent chunks of work — resizing four images, handling four incoming requests — can run at the literal same instant on different cores, only possible with multiple schedulable entities.
- **Resource sharing without IPC**: threads in a web server can share a connection pool or an in-memory cache directly through shared heap memory, with no serialization or IPC overhead — exactly the kind of sharing that would need explicit shared memory or message passing between separate processes.

The unifying theme: threads buy you concurrency and shared state cheaply, in exchange for having to manage that shared state carefully.

| | Processes | Threads |
|---|---|---|
| Address space | Separate, isolated | Shared within the process |
| Communication | Needs explicit IPC (pipes, shared memory, sockets) | Direct — shared heap and globals |
| Creation cost | Higher — new address space, page tables | Lower — reuses the process's address space |
| Context switch cost | Higher — often flushes TLB, swaps page tables | Lower — no page table swap needed |
| Fault isolation | A crash in one process doesn't take down another | A crash in one thread (bad pointer, unhandled exception) can take down the whole process |
| Typical use | Isolation-critical, independently-deployed units | Tightly-coupled concurrent work sharing state |

The fault-isolation row is the one interviewers probe most: threads trade isolation for cheapness, so a design choosing threads over processes is implicitly accepting that a bug in any one thread can corrupt or crash everything else in that process.

slides.sectionTitle: Thread creation cost vs process creation cost
slides.markdown:
Creating a process (`fork()`) means allocating a new PCB, setting up new page tables, and — even with copy-on-write — doing real kernel bookkeeping to establish a distinct address space. Creating a thread (`pthread_create()` or a language's thread-spawn call) reuses the existing process's address space entirely and only has to allocate a new stack and register set, which is dramatically less work.

As a rough order of magnitude that shows up often in interview discussions: thread creation is commonly cited as roughly **10-100x cheaper** than process creation on typical Unix systems, though the exact ratio depends heavily on OS and workload. This is why a server handling a high rate of short-lived units of work (a request per connection) almost always reaches for a thread pool rather than forking a process per request.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming threads are "free" — shared-state bugs are the price
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Threads are cheaper than processes, so I should just use as many threads as possible and let them all touch shared data — it'll be fine, they're all part of the same program."

**Why it's wrong:** cheapness of creation says nothing about the cost of correctness. Two threads incrementing the same counter without synchronization can lose updates (a classic **race condition**) even though each individual increment looks trivially safe in isolation. The bugs this produces are often non-deterministic — they show up under load in production and are notoriously hard to reproduce locally, exactly because thread scheduling order isn't fixed.

**Correct model:** every piece of shared mutable state accessed by more than one thread needs an explicit synchronization plan (a lock, an atomic operation, or a design that avoids sharing it at all) — "it's just a thread" is not a safety argument. The real cost of threads isn't creation time, it's the ongoing engineering discipline required to keep shared state correct.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: how many threads is too many?
slides.markdown:
Threads aren't infinitely cheap either. Each thread needs its own stack — often defaulting to **1-8MB of reserved virtual address space** per thread (configurable, and much of it may never be touched thanks to demand paging, but it still counts against per-process limits and, if actually used, real memory). Spawn tens of thousands of threads and you can exhaust address space or hit OS thread-count limits well before you exhaust CPU.

There's also a scheduling cost: beyond roughly the number of CPU cores, additional *runnable* threads don't add parallelism, just context-switch overhead, as the scheduler now has more entities time-slicing the same cores. This is the concrete reason production systems use bounded **thread pools** (say, sized to 2-4x core count for I/O-bound work) rather than spawning a fresh thread per request — unbounded thread creation under load is a classic way to turn a traffic spike into a full outage.

slides.sectionTitle: The staff-level framing: threads and processes are complementary, not competing
slides.markdown:
A junior answer treats "threads vs processes" as pick-one. A senior answer recognizes most real systems use **both**, at different granularities. Nginx and PostgreSQL both run a pool of worker *processes* for fault isolation — one worker crashing doesn't take the whole server down — while many application frameworks run a pool of *threads* within each of those processes to share connection pools, caches, and in-memory state cheaply.

The general pattern worth stating out loud in an interview: use process boundaries where you need genuine fault isolation or independent deployability, and thread boundaries where you need cheap, high-throughput sharing of state within one unit of isolation — and be explicit about which failure you're willing to accept at each boundary.
